touches.text: QUESTIONS: a question is [Q#n: ...], placed at the line it bears on. Its #n is its own and never changes; a new one takes the next unused number, which is now 127. An answered question disappears: its answer is folded into the intention and why (0.2.1), and signed where it records a decision (0.5). Why? Becuase too many words makes it hard for both akien and Claude to understand.

An artifact is present tense or past tense, never both. Present tense is rewritten whole and points at its provenance; past tense is append-only, opened when needed, and read cold only through a compiled face (state, the latest slate). WHY: what a cold reader loads at an address should be what is true now.

artifact: the one door a record of truth changes through, and the journal of who came through it (hash-chained, caller read from the kernel). WHY: errors are permanent in records of truth (Law 7), and the journal is what shows a record moved by hand. USERS: everyone who writes a record.

question: the open-question door: a decision only the operator can make, bound to its ticket, answered in the operator's words. WHY: a spec choice is settled by Akien's head, recorded verbatim, never by a paragraph of CC's. USERS: tickets and CodeMother open them; the operator answers (7.4.2).

dataref: one address for any stored record, in any format, and the thin class that reads it. WHY: a config, a ticket or a node can say WHERE a value lives without carrying it, so the repo stays shareable and a private value stays in ~/.cairn; and one way of pointing works across every format and every box. USERS: anything that reads stored data.
One that does not resolve is loud and names its address, never a value. A sieve reds a class-space config holding a plain value where a secret belongs.

A proof MAY read the live database; what a test writes stays out of live, either in the TESTING database or marked as a testing artifact that the rest of the system ignores. WHY: reading live saves populating test data; ignoring testing artifacts keeps them from leaking into what the system believes. Test against live, marked as testing. -amm

How the TESTING database works. (1) The db proxy is the seam (4.3.1.5.1.4.1.1, 11.3.7): proofs, devices and tools never choose a database; the proxy chooses by session context. (2) The test runner sets the context, never the proof: bin/cairn test and the hollow run open every db session with context=testing, so a proof can neither forget it nor pick live (Law 4). (3) In testing context, writes go only to the TESTING database: same schema, rows from a reserved address range, so a testing address never collides with a live one. (4) In testing context, reads are an overlay: testing rows first, live underneath, live pinned at the seq the run started at. A proof reads live with no fixtures, what it wrote shadows live for that run only, and the run repeats within itself. (5) In live context the proxy never consults the TESTING database, so testing artifacts are invisible to all but the run that made them, by construction rather than by filtering. (6) Each run's testing rows carry its run id and are dropped at run end; the sleep cycle sweeps orphans. (7) A proof over live data asserts invariants, never snapshots; a tooth that needs an exact value writes its fixture into the overlay first. Until the per-box proxy exists, the same routing sits in the store door (db_domain) and moves into the proxy when it is built. WHY: a context the proof sets is a context a proof can forget; the runner is the one place every proof passes through. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator -amm
Test tiers: commit, hourly, daily and weekly. Each tier runs only what it must, so a commit needs only its own proofs and the long runs wait for the long tiers; nothing runs just in case.

The memory model. Everything Cairn keeps as LEARNING in database memory is these five things, and only these. Logs, troubles, git records and a device's own state keep their own homes (4.3.2-4.3.4). WHY: one kind of access everywhere.

The scheme names the root; the path finds the record; the part after # finds the item inside it. Each root is found on the box it runs on, so one address works on Linux, on Windows and on a fresh machine.

A Dataref reads; it never writes. A write goes through the owner's gate (Law 6), and a db: address is read through db_domain's own client, never a second dial to 5432. An address on another box is read over the bus. WHY: one address system must not become one back door.
Questions live here and nowhere else. The questions/ inbox and `cairn question` are deprecated for now. -amm
Shareable provenance (charters, tickets, validations) is git JSON beside the code, never a row.

A ticket's plan is a plan, not a list of decisions: constraints, outcomes and resources. - Outcomes, not tasks: each is a claim a proof can check. An outcome hides the how. - Constraints: the bounds, and every how Akien is attached to (encapsulation, the bus as the only channel). - Order comes only from real dependencies (you can't test the bus envelope shape until the bus works), and those also set ticket order. - Resources: existing machines, tools and design patterns, named when they need stating. - A plan too big splits into tickets. Early steps can reshape later ones, so the whole is checked for coherence at the end. -amm

A file Dataref keeps its value and re-reads only when the file's modification time, size or inode has changed (a stat reads no data; a write that replaces the file in one step gets a new inode, which catches a change where timestamps are coarse). A Secret keeps nothing between reads. A db Dataref does not cache until a measured need asks for it. HYPOTHESIS: it will be read often enough for the cache to pay; the reads are counted (a metric, 17.27) to find out.

conflicts.ticket_says: Modifies question records stored in CairnCommons/questions/open-*.json separate files, with measured and measured_resolves_nowhere fields
conflicts.why: 0.6.2 declares 'Questions live here and nowhere else' (in the outline as [Q#n] entries). The ticket treats questions as persistent data structures in separate files outside the outline. This violates the stated boundary that questions exist only in the outline. While 0.6.2 acknowledges the old questions/ system is 'deprecated for now', the outline's absolute claim contradicts storing questions elsewhere, even in deprecated infrastructure.
